title: Trickle-down AI: Safe ground for AI in education
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Matthews proposes 'trickle-down AI' as stable ground for schools amid AI-driven destabilisation: the teacher uses AI at the desk to produce resources, and students receive the benefit without using AI themselves. His premise is that teachers and students are not in the same position, since teachers have the experience and organic intelligence needed to use AI wisely while students are still building them. He points to preparation tasks that are pedagogically necessary but administratively costly, such as adjusting the length and complexity of readings, writing sentence stems and building retrieval quizzes, and argues AI makes these cheaper to do for more students. He does not abandon student use of AI but says it has more variables and fewer obvious wins, and that the principle 'you cannot automate what you don't understand' applies to novices. Where AI use by students is unwanted, he suggests device-free lessons. A short piece, but with a clear thesis on where schools should start.
points: Trickle-down AI locates the benefit of AI in teacher-side resource creation, so students gain without using AI themselves.
The case rests on teachers and students being differently placed: adult expertise is a prerequisite for using AI wisely.
Concrete uses named are sentence stems, retrieval practice quizzes and re-levelling texts, which are necessary but time-consuming tasks.
Student AI use is not ruled out but carries more variables, and classroom practices such as device-free lessons are needed to make intent enforceable.
The recommended entry point for schools unsure how to integrate AI is simple teacher training in making high-quality resources.
quotes: Many of the load-bearing pillars our schools rested upon are wobbling. Access to information, assessment, classroom practice, romance and relationships have all been changed significantly because of AI.
In this vision, the teacher uses AI to create resources and design learning. The AI use happens at the teacher’s desk. The resources are generated and then distributed to the students.

But to actually develop these qualities, students need to do the hard work of learning, growth, and developing their organic intelligence. And if we aren’t careful, AI can actually hinder the process, not enhance it.

Our planning and preparation are full of tasks that are pedagogically necessary but administratively taxing. Consider the simple task of reducing the length and complexity of an in-class reading. We’ve been doing this for generations, but it is costly.

We can create the same kind of resources that we’ve always made, but create them more efficiently for more students. They’re still pedagogically necessary, but perhaps not so administratively taxing anymore.

But then we should be clear about when and where they use it, and set up classroom practices which help them make good decisions about AI use. For example, if I didn’t want my students to use AI, I might run my lessons device-free.
With simple training they can create high-quality resources that welcome each learner into the learning. The resources can be tailored, differentiated, and aligned with the school vision.
